Date: 2026-09-03
Time: 09:05 PDT / 16:05 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jared Porter (Redwood SE), Rohit Nair (Redwood Product), Elena Voss (Lucid Harbor Head of AI), Marco Reyes (Lucid Harbor Backend), Priya Iyer (Lucid Harbor SRE)
Links shared: https://redwood.ai/decks/optimize-prefetch-demo (deck), https://redwood.ai/sheets/cost-model-lucid (cost model spreadsheet), sandbox request form: https://redwood.ai/sandbox-request
summary: High-level Optimize walkthrough focused on combining prefix (KV) caching and dynamic batching to reduce token-unit costs while meeting a 120–150ms p95 latency budget. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated; primary concerns: data residency, SSO/SAML, KMS, and deterministic tail latency. Agreed to a 2-week sandbox and to share cost model spreadsheet. SE to run perf sim with their traces.
topics: Prefetch vs session cache tradeoffs; ideal batch size windows; prefix/KV hit lifecycle; cold-starts and warmup; concurrency and autoscale burst; routing to cheaper model variants under load; SSO/KMS questions; pricing sensitivity scenarios
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: okay hi everybody welcome, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, Jared's here on the SE side, Rohit from product. how's everyone doing?
[00:08] Elena Voss: good, thank you, excited — we been digging into your docs and the cost models looked promising.
[00:12] Marco Reyes: morning all. quick note we have 600rps peak for search assistant, but median is about 70, and sessions last 40 to 90 tokens typically.
[00:22] Jared Porter: awesome, that helps. so today we'll run through the Optimize console, then show the prefetched KV example and how batching interacts with prefix hits, and end with an econ sim for your workload.
[00:33] Priya Iyer: quick ask — our SLA requires 150ms p95 on text generation for 90% of calls. Is that realistic with heavy prefetch?
[00:42] Jared Porter: short answer, yes with constraints. long answer: prefix caching can take most of the decoder cost off the hot path if you can precompute common prompts; batching then reduces per-token compute on remaining suffixes. the trick is warmup and the hit rate.
[00:55] Marco Reyes: when you say prefix caching you mean Redwood's KV cache where we store the cached key/value pairs for attention? sometimes our infra folks call that the K V cache, others call session cache.
[01:05] Jared Porter: yeah both terms used. in the console it's labeled "Prefix KV cache (lookahead)". you can configure TTL, hot-tier capacity, and look-ahead depth.
[01:14] Elena Voss: can you show the console flow?
[01:17] Jared Porter: sure sharing screen now - bear with occasional lag. so here's the Optimize tab, on the left we have workload profiles — I'm loading a sample profile named "lucid-sim-70rps" that Maya pre-seeded.
[01:30] [screen show noise, brief silence]
[01:35] Jared Porter: ok visible — first pane: cache policy. you can set prefetch rules (e.g., prefetch top 200 most common prompts per minute), TTL 1h/6h/24h, and fallback routing. the cost sim on the right will estimate tokens saved and dollars per month. you'll notice we calc both GPU time saved and token-unit reductions.
[01:52] Elena Voss: in our pilot we saw inconsistent cache hits, sometimes cold starts killed latency — do you recommend fixed prefetch vs adaptive?
[01:59] Jared Porter: in most consumer chat flows adaptive prefetch works best — we prefetch entries as the session heatmap predicts next-turn prompts. for high-variance workflows, fixed scheduled prefetch of top N prompts gives more predictable tail latency.
[02:12] Marco Reyes: can we feed our historical traces? we want realistic sim numbers.
[02:16] Maya Chen: yes please — Marco if you can share traces (Sanitized) Jared can drop them into the sandbox model runner. that's actually one of the next steps.
[02:25] Priya Iyer: on encryption — if we run sandbox in Redwood hosted, how's the KMS handled? we need CMK control ideally.
[02:33] Rohit Nair: good question. hosted supports customer-managed keys via our KMS integrations; for Private deployments you keep full on-prem HSM. for the sandbox we'll provide ephemeral keys but we can scope a dedicated KMS flow for evaluation.
[02:45] Elena Voss: SOC2 mention? our procurement asks for SOC2 Type II.
[02:49] Maya Chen: Redwood has SOC2 Type II in the enterprise package, we can attach our compliance pack to the SOW. I'll send the compliance docs in the follow-up.
[02:58] Marco Reyes: thanks. back to batching — what batch sizes do you recommend for 70rps median and 600rps peak?
[03:05] Jared Porter: it depends on your suffix lengths. for short suffixes (<=60 tokens) and a 70rps median, dynamic batching with window 5–15ms and max batch size 16 often gives the best latency/cost tradeoff. under peak 600rps we route to dedicated pools and increase concurrency — batches can grow to 64 but you need to accept some p95 increase.
[03:25] Elena Voss: is that concurrency per model? we have multi-tenant endpoints today.
[03:29] Jared Porter: yes per model instance. Redwood routing supports model routing by tenant; you can pin a tenant to a dedicated pool to prevent noisy neighbor effects.
[03:37] Marco Reyes: you mentioned routing to cheaper model variants — e.g., fall back from a 13B quantized to a 7B in high load?
[03:43] Jared Porter: exactly. policy-based routing lets you specify latency/cost tradeoffs; on overload we can route non-critical calls to a faster, cheaper model variant. the console will simulate QoS impact.
[03:53] Priya Iyer: what about prefix eviction and TTL? if an evicted prefix is requested again we pay both token cost and latency for rehydration, right?
[04:01] Jared Porter: correct. eviction strategy is LRU by default, but we expose hot-tier pinning for business-critical prompts. you can also set a grace warmup: when eviction predicted, we prefetch to reduce rehydration pain.
[04:12] Elena Voss: can you show a concrete example with our typical search prompt?
[04:16] Jared Porter: sure loading the sample trace — here's a user flow where the first 30 tokens are identical across many queries (the system prompt + product taxonomy). with prefix hits we remove about 42% of decoder compute, batching adds another 28% token efficiency. net token reduction ~60% in the sim.
[04:35] [brief hesitation, audio artifact]
[04:40] Marco Reyes: 60% sounds high. what's the baseline assumptions?
[04:43] Jared Porter: baseline assumed single-request cold decoder, no caching, cpu-affine scheduling. our sim uses your trace's QPS distribution — the most important lever is prefix hit rate; at 35–40% hit rate we hit that 50–60% area.
[04:57] Elena Voss: what do we need to change in our app to get those hits?
[05:01] Marco Reyes: little pause
[05:02] Priya Iyer: we can't change user prompts; can you normalize?
[05:05] Jared Porter: yes normalization + canonicalization are key: strip session metadata, map aliases, and maintain a small set of canonical prompts. Redwood has a helper lib that runs client-side or in our ingestion pipeline to map similar prompts to canonical keys. that drives hit-rate up a lot.
[05:18] Elena Voss: any risk to output quality when canonicalizing?
[05:22] Jared Porter: minimal if done conservatively — we only canonicalize deterministic prefix content. it's a safety-first approach.
[05:27] Maya Chen: Rohit — product note, we can provide an SDK snippet to show canonicalization rules.
[05:31] Rohit Nair: yeah we'll include an example rule set in the sandbox package.
[05:35] Marco Reyes: latency numbers? if we hit prefix locally is it sub-50ms?
[05:39] Jared Porter: in our hosted profile prefix-hit + small suffix decode is typically 60–120ms depending on model size. sub-50ms is rare unless you're on on-prem ultra-low-latency hardware. with dedicated GPU pools and pinning you can get tighter tail numbers.
[05:51] Elena Voss: we are leaning hosted for speed of adoption but worried about data residency. any intermediate options?
[05:58] Maya Chen: we offer Private VPC options, and a hybrid where control plane is Redwood-hosted but data plane sits in your cloud region. that can solve residency and KMS concerns.
[06:08] Priya Iyer: our security team also wants SSO with SAML and RBAC per-route.
[06:12] Maya Chen: SAML SSO is supported enterprise tier; route-level RBAC is in the enterprise RBAC add-on. we'll include that in the compliance pack.
[06:21] Marco Reyes: about the simulator — can the console simulate costs if we turn on 2-second lookahead prefetch?
[06:27] Jared Porter: yes, lookahead depth is a parameter. increasing lookahead increases prefetching cost (extra tokens precomputed) but can improve hit-rate and reduce tail latency. the cost sim shows net delta. for your traces, a 2-second lookahead improved hit-rate from 28% to 46% in our last run, net savings of ~22% in token spend.
[06:44] Elena Voss: nice. any caveats for streaming outputs? we stream to web clients, does prefix caching change streaming behavior?
[06:51] Jared Porter: streaming remains supported; prefix caching only changes compute on the backend. you still get chunked responses. small detail: if you use KV cache to skip early tokens, streaming might begin slightly faster because less compute is queued.
[07:04] Marco Reyes: what do you log for audit — do we get token-level logs or just aggregate?
[07:08] Rohit Nair: both. we log token-level telemetry in the enterprise plan (with retention controls). we can redact user text but keep perf and cost metrics for billing reconciliation.
[07:18] Elena Voss: are there any public benchmark artifacts for latency vs quantization?
[07:22] Maya Chen: yes I'll share the latency matrix deck — link in the header.
[07:26] Marco Reyes: hypothetical question: if we go dedicated, what's the sizing guidance for 600rps peak and your batch windows?
[07:33] Jared Porter: rough thumb: for a 13B quantized model, assume 1 GPU can handle ~150-200 effective rps with batching tuned; so for 600rps peak we'd recommend a 3–4 GPU pool with autoscale headroom and pinning for critical tenants. the console will give a more precise calc when you upload traces.
[07:50] Priya Iyer: on pricing: how much does prefetch increase our monthly spend?
[07:54] Maya Chen: it depends. prefetch adds compute (you're precomputing tokens), but when it converts to higher hit rate it reduces decode cost and often nets savings. that's why we run per-workload sims — we'll send the spreadsheet with toggles.
[08:06] Marco Reyes: ok let's talk deliverables and timeline. we want to evaluate in 2 weeks and see a clear ROI case.
[08:12] Maya Chen: plan: 1) we enable sandbox and load your traces; 2) SE runs a perf sim and returns 3 scenarios (conservative, expected, aggressive); 3) we'll do a follow-up deep-dive with Priya on latency tuning.
[08:23] Elena Voss: sounds good. one more small ask: can you include an example of a canonicalization rule to share with our frontend team?
[08:28] Jared Porter: yes we'll add a snippet in the sandbox repo.
[08:31] [several people talking briefly: "great", "thanks"]
[08:34] Maya Chen: ok quick recap — Maya to send deck and spreadsheet, Jared to provision sandbox and load traces, Marco to share traces. follow-up deep-dive scheduled shallow for next week. any objections?
[08:44] Marco Reyes: no objections. thanks everyone.
[08:46] Elena Voss: thanks, excited to see the sim numbers.
[08:48] Maya Chen: thanks all, we'll follow up in email. bye.
[08:52] [call ends]

Notes on transcript quality: several short audio glitches and one screen-share hiccup during the console demo; some proper nouns (KMS, KV) transcribed as separate characters."
